mission.name: Would You Merge This AI-Generated PR?
mission.seoTitle: AI Code Review Mission — Review Agent-Generated Code | AhaFrame
mission.description: Review an AI-generated pull request that passes tests but hides an architectural regression. Inspect evidence, tighten the coding policy, rerun, compare, and decide whether to merge.
mission.hero: Your coding agent changed 17 files. CI is green. The diff looks plausible. One architectural boundary is still broken. Decide whether the evidence is strong enough to merge.
mission.quick: AI-generated code should be judged against an explicit change contract, repository architecture, targeted tests, and dependency evidence—not against how convincing the diff looks.

brief.title: Green tests are not a merge decision.
brief.role: You are the engineer responsible for the merge.
brief.body: An agent implemented a cache optimization and added a dependency. Existing tests pass, but the generated change bypasses a transaction boundary and touches unrelated files. The PR is fast to accept and expensive to misunderstand.
brief.objective: Reduce regression and architecture risk while keeping review effort bounded.
brief.stakes: If the hidden boundary violation ships, production can serve stale state after a successful transaction.

ui.waiting: Inspect the evidence, change the review policy, then evaluate the PR.

debrief.title: The review target is the system contract, not the generated patch.
debrief.rule: Passing tests are evidence, not proof that generated code belongs in the repository.
debrief.body: AI coding compresses implementation time and expands verification responsibility. A strong workflow bounds the requested change, checks architectural invariants, creates tests for the new behavior and likely failure modes, and reviews dependency movement. This turns AI code review from aesthetic approval into an evidence process.
points: Write the change contract before judging the generated implementation.
Review repository-level invariants that line-by-line diff inspection can miss.
Generate tests from risks, not only from the happy-path specification.
Treat new dependencies as part of the architecture decision.

takeaways: A stable target makes it possible to tell whether the agent solved the requested problem or merely produced plausible code.
Green CI only proves what the current test suite checks.
Most expensive regressions occur where generated changes violate architecture, data or operational contracts.
